text.title: Inference Cost Unit Economics Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every inference cost unit economics report MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: The headline metric per feature MUST be cost per successful outcome: the sum of every call made in service of that outcome (including retries, fallbacks, validation failures and abandoned sessions) divided by the count of outcomes that met the feature's success definition from step 1 of the procedure. Cost per call and cost per token MAY appear only as supporting lines, never as the headline.

rationale.source: SaaS unit-economics practice (cost per unit of value delivered); widely established in AI product finance

rule.rationale: A support bot that costs $0.04 per call and needs eleven calls plus two retries per resolved ticket costs $0.52 per resolution, not $0.04. Reports that lead with cost per call systematically understate the number finance will later find in the invoice, and every pricing decision built on them is wrong in the same direction.

rule.statement: Every per-call cost MUST be decomposed into at least four separately priced lines: input tokens x input price, output tokens x output price, retrieval (embedding calls plus vector-store queries), and tool or function calls (external API cost). Where the provider bills cached or batch input at a different rate, cached tokens MUST be a fifth line. A single undifferentiated "LLM cost" figure is rejected.

rationale.source: Provider price sheets (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) bill input, output and cached tokens at distinct rates

rule.rationale: Output tokens typically cost several times input tokens, and cached input a fraction of uncached. A blended number hides which lever matters: a feature whose cost is 80% output tokens is fixed by shortening the answer format, one whose cost is 80% retrieval is fixed by cutting top-k. Without the split the team optimises the prompt when the problem was the reranker.

rule.statement: Token counts MUST be taken from the provider-reported usage object on each API response (for example `usage.input_tokens` / `usage.output_tokens` or `usage.prompt_tokens` / `usage.completion_tokens`), logged per call with the model id. Estimating tokens from character or word counts, or sampling a subset and extrapolating, is forbidden for the report figures.

rationale.source: OpenAI and Anthropic API responses carry a per-request `usage` object; provider documentation

rule.rationale: Character-based estimates miss system prompts, tool schemas, injected retrieval context and provider-side formatting, which together are usually the majority of input tokens. Teams that estimate routinely report a third of the tokens the invoice shows and then cannot explain the gap to finance.

rule.statement: The report MUST state, per feature, the share of total cost caused by retries, fallbacks to a larger model, and calls whose output failed validation, as a percentage. When that share exceeds 15% the report MUST flag retry policy as the first action and MUST NOT recommend prompt or model changes for that feature until the retry cause is named.

rationale.source: Methodology decision gate (04-procedure step 3); widely established practice in LLM operations

rule.rationale: Retries are invisible in per-call dashboards because each retry is its own successful-looking call. One team cut their prompt by 30% and saw no cost change because 40% of spend was an exponential-backoff loop on a rate-limited tool call. The 15% gate makes that visible before anyone touches the prompt.

rule.statement: Every unit price used MUST cite the provider, the exact model id (including the dated snapshot where the provider publishes one), the price-sheet date or URL it was read from, and any negotiated, committed-use or batch discount applied. List prices without a date, or a "blended" rate without its derivation, are rejected.

rationale.source: Provider pricing pages change without notice; provider documentation

rule.rationale: Providers reprice models, retire snapshots and introduce cheaper tiers on a cadence of weeks. A margin report computed on last quarter's price sheet can be off by a factor of two in either direction, and nobody can tell which without the date. Pinning the sheet turns "our cost went up" into a diff.

rule.statement: Gross margin per feature MUST be computed as (revenue or value proxy minus fully loaded inference cost) divided by revenue, and the report MUST name the revenue basis per feature: directly attributed revenue, an allocation rule (with the allocation key), or a value proxy with its derivation. A margin figure whose revenue basis is unstated is rejected.

rationale.source: Standard gross-margin definition; SaaS metrics practice

rule.rationale: A feature inside a bundled subscription has no invoice line of its own, so its "revenue" is always a modelling choice. When two reports pick different allocation keys they produce margins of 40% and 85% for the same feature. Stating the basis is what lets a reader compare quarters and challenge the model instead of the arithmetic.

rule.statement: Cost per outcome MUST be reported as a distribution: p50, p95 and mean at minimum, computed over a stated window of at least seven days of production traffic. A feature whose p95 exceeds 5x its p50 MUST be flagged as tail-dominated with the tail driver named (long context, agent loops, tool retries).

rationale.source: Google SRE Book, ch. Monitoring Distributed Systems, on percentiles versus averages

rule.rationale: Agentic and long-context features have heavy tails: most sessions are cheap and a few percent run twenty tool calls with a full document in context. The mean sits well above the median and moves with a handful of users. Pricing on the mean overcharges everyone; pricing on the median loses money on the tail. Only the distribution shows which.

rule.statement: Every feature in the report MUST carry a cost ceiling per outcome derived from its target gross margin and revenue basis, plus an alert threshold on daily spend (absolute amount or percentage over trailing 7-day baseline) wired to the observability pipeline. The report MUST list every feature whose actual cost per outcome exceeds its ceiling with the gap and the owner of the corrective action.

rationale.source: FinOps Foundation framework (budgeting and anomaly management capabilities)

rule.rationale: Inference spend has no natural cap: a prompt regression, a looping agent or a viral usage spike can multiply daily cost overnight and the first signal is the monthly invoice. A ceiling turns the margin target into a number an alert can fire on, so the runaway is caught in hours rather than at quarter close.
